deed: Israelis install solar water pumps in African villages — six million people receive clean water
title: Sivan Yaari's Israeli nonprofit pumps clean water with solar power to villages in Africa

trailer.text: According to ynet, she founded the organization after a visit to Africa, where she saw poverty, hunger and disease, and a lack of clean water and electricity.
According to the Jerusalem Post, Innovation: Africa is an Israeli nonprofit, and it provides solar-powered clean water to remote communities in Sub-Saharan Africa.
In each village the organization drills into the groundwater, installs a solar pump, builds a 10-meter tower and carries the water to taps throughout the village.
According to JNS, when the taps were opened in the village of Nyamphanza in Zambia, the cumulative number of people whose lives had changed since 2008 passed 5 million.

stations.title: Hours of walking for a little water

paragraphs.text: According to the organization's website, over 400 million people in Africa do not have access to clean water.
According to the website, they remain trapped in poverty and disease, without education and without economic opportunities.
According to JNS, mainly women and children are tasked with bringing water.
Sometimes they walk enormous distances to open, contaminated water sources, and little time is left for school.
Yaari recounted that she saw people walking for hours on foot and digging in puddles with their hands to find a little contaminated water.
A local leader from the village of Nyamphanza in Zambia said that the community had to drink from a water source it shared with animals.
According to JNS, at the time the article was published Zambia was facing its worst drought in at least two decades, and a state of national emergency had been declared.
According to ISRAEL21c, in February 2017 Yaari and her staff met residents in the village of Akuyam in Uganda who had not eaten for three days.

stations.title: From Rishon LeZion to a clinic in Tanzania

paragraphs.text: Yaari was born in Rishon LeZion to a family of limited means, according to ynet.
Her father immigrated from Algiers, and her mother came from Tunis.
According to ynet, at the age of 20 she received a job offer from Israeli businessman Rafi Nakash, owner of the Jordache group.
According to ynet, she founded the organization after returning from a visit to Africa, where she was exposed to poverty, hunger, disease and a lack of clean water and electricity.
Yaari recounted that during a UN internship in Senegal they found that most of the generators were not working, because there was no fuel or because they were broken.
According to ynet, as a student Yaari returned to a village in Tanzania and installed two solar panels at the clinic.
The panels produced electricity, and thanks to them a refrigerator for medicines and vaccines could be brought into the clinic.
According to the FAQ on the organization's website, Innovation: Africa was established in 2008.

stations.title: How water is brought to a village

paragraphs.text: Yaari described the process as follows: they drill into the groundwater, build a tower and install the solar panels at its top.
According to the organization's website, the drilling into the aquifer is done with local contractors.
Then they install a submersible solar pump, build a 10-meter tower and distribute the water in the village to up to 15 taps.
According to the Jerusalem Post, the towers hold the panels and the water tank.
According to the organization, after successful drilling a water sample is sent to a laboratory for comprehensive analysis.
According to the Jerusalem Post, distribution points are built throughout the village so that all community members have equal access to water, sometimes as many as 10,000 people.
According to the FAQ on the website, a water project costs up to $65,000 for a village of at least 3,000 people.
According to JNS, each of the more than 1,000 villages the organization has connected pumps an average of 15,000 liters of clean water a day.
Not every drilling succeeds right away. Yaari recounted one drilling that succeeded only on the 13th attempt, and then the residents burst into dancing and shouts of joy.

stations.title: Israeli technology and a remote eye

paragraphs.text: According to the organization's website, the work is powered by Israeli technology and real-time project data.
Yaari said that the organization buys only Israeli technology, for example an Israeli battery and inverter.
According to a publication of the Embassy of Tanzania, the organization's "energy box" contains lithium-ion batteries, an inverter, a charge controller and LED bulbs, all produced in Israel.
According to JNS, proprietary monitoring technology detects aberrations in the water supply and reports them to a local team that can address the problem.
According to the organization's website, the remote monitoring system won a UN award.
With it, donors can track live the amount of water pumped or energy produced.
According to the organization, 100% of every donation goes to a project, because a group of donors covers the operating costs.
Yaari said that at some of the clinics where energy had been installed, residents come from the surrounding villages to charge their cell phones, paying 10 to 15 cents.
The money is used to buy bulbs and replace batteries.

stations.title: The people who build and maintain

paragraphs.text: According to JNS, in Nyamphanza the local contractor hired 10 residents, paid them and trained them.
According to the organization, trainees receive a certificate of completion that helps them find work in the future.
Dickson Piri of Nyamphanza learned construction in the training program and said he is willing to teach others what he learned.
According to JNS, the program teaches local community leaders, project managers and engineers to maintain the technologies, so that they are self-reliant.
According to JNS, 24 local employees of the organization came to Israel for a two-week training course in innovation and community development.
According to JNS, most of the engineers on the organization's team are African.
According to the FAQ on the website, the employees, among them engineers and field officers, are based in Africa.
Yaari said that in most of the villages they reach, the Israeli team are the first Israelis the residents meet.
According to the organization, clean water improves residents' health, eliminates waterborne diseases, raises school attendance and frees women from the task of fetching water.
According to the organization, following the water, businesses such as brick-making and agricultural programs are established, and residents sell surplus vegetables in markets.
Helen Njobvu of Nyamphanza said that with clean water she will be able to grow vegetables to eat and to sell, and earn money.
According to JNS, in Uganda the panels, pumps, tanks and taps brought clean drinking water to villages whose residents walked about three hours for non-contaminated water.
According to ISRAEL21c, an Israeli bar mitzvah celebrant contributed $18,000 to power a primary school in Uganda attended by 1,000 students.

According to ISRAEL21c, Karamoja in Uganda is the region that was discussed with Herzl in 1903 as a possible refuge for Jews, but the land actually offered to Herzl was in British East Africa, today's Kenya, not in Uganda.
Abraham Ngobeni of South Africa recounted that 11 projects were completed within six months, and that women no longer need to walk far for water.
According to the Jerusalem Post, the organization worked with UNICEF Cameroon to provide solar power, clean water and healthcare to tens of thousands of refugees.

According to ISRAEL21c, among those benefiting from a joint project of the organization and UNICEF in Cameroon are 250,000 refugees from the Central African Republic. The project included pumping water in Bertoua, supplying solar power to three clinics and installing a solar water-pumping system in one village.
According to ynet, in the year before the article another 230 villages were connected, despite the coronavirus pandemic.
According to JNS, in early May the taps were opened in Nyamphanza, and the cumulative number of people whose lives had changed since 2008 passed 5 million.
Years earlier, at a ceremony marking the organization's tenth anniversary, Yaari told JNS that although the organization had helped more than a million people, it was only a drop in the ocean.
According to the encyclopedia Encyclopedia.com, Joseph Chamberlain, the British colonial secretary, offered Herzl the Guas Ngishu plateau in East Africa.

According to ISRAEL21c, in 2012 the organization was granted Special Consultative Status at the UN Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC), and the following year it won the Innovation Award at the UN development expo in Nairobi.
Yaari was selected to light a torch at the ceremony for Israel's 75th Independence Day in 2023.
In October 2026 she received an honorary doctorate from Bar-Ilan University, at the university's 70th gala.

stations.title: What is hard along the way

paragraphs.text: Yaari said that what worries her most is repeated drilling that does not find water, while the residents watch anxiously.
She recounted a young woman who said she had no milk and no water.
According to ynet, Yaari said she sent the drill, but it was not fast enough, and the baby died two days later.
Yaari said in an interview with ynet that the organization had already helped more than 500 villages, and added that it sounds like a lot but it is not.
She recounted that some people tell her there is enough poverty in Israel, and ask why she goes to Africa.
Yaari replied that she herself experienced poverty in Israel and so that is true, but she found an accessible solution to a different kind of poverty.

disagreements.question: How many people has the organization reached?

versions.says: JNS: more than 5 million people since 2008
FAQ on the organization's website: over 3.8 million people in 10 countries
Jerusalem Post: more than 4.2 million people, in over 880 installations
ynet: at least three million people
Publication of the Embassy of Tanzania (June 2019): more than one and a half million people

disagreements.question: How many villages has the organization connected?

versions.says: JNS: more than 1,000 villages
Yaari in an interview with ynet, about 13 years after the organization was founded: more than 500 villages

disagreements.question: In how many African countries does the organization operate?

versions.says: ynet: six countries in which the organization has a representative office with local staff, and projects in four more countries.
FAQ on the organization's website: 10 countries, and the organization is now expanding to Rwanda

disagreements.question: How many employees does the organization have?

versions.says: Organization's website: more than 100 full-time employees, mostly engineers, and 50 local contractors
FAQ on the organization's website: over 140 full-time employees
JNS: a team of 150 engineers
Jerusalem Post: more than 130 employees, among them more than 80 hydrologists and engineers, as well as over 40 local contractors

disagreements.question: What does the organization aim to reach?

versions.says: JNS: nearly 8 million people by 2027
Jerusalem Post: another 1,200 projects and 10 million people in the next four years

disagreements.question: How many people in Africa are still without clean water?

versions.says: Organization's website, and also Yaari to JNS: more than 400 million people
Yaari to ynet: more than 450 million people whom the organization has not yet reached

disagreements.question: How many refugees did the organization's joint project with UNICEF in Cameroon reach?

versions.says: Jerusalem Post, quoting Yaari: tens of thousands of refugees
ISRAEL21c: 250,000 refugees from the Central African Republic

disagreements.question: What did Yaari do to help the young mother in Karamoja?

versions.says: ynet: Yaari sent the drill, but it was not fast enough
YPO: Yaari drove six hours south to fill a van with beans, maize and water, and by the time she came back it was too late

disagreements.question: How much does a village water project cost?

versions.says: FAQ on the organization's website: up to $65,000 for a village of at least 3,000 people
The organization's homepage: sponsor a whole village for $85,000

claims.text: לפי ynet, יערי הקימה את הארגון לאחר שחזרה מביקור באפריקה, שם נחשפה לעוני, רעב ומחלות ולמחסור בתשתיות בסיסיות, בעיקר מים נקיים וחשמל.

claims.quote: Innovation: Africa is a non-profit transforming lives by delivering solar-powered clean water to remote communities across Sub-Saharan Africa.

claims.text: בפרויקט מים הארגון קודח לאקוויפר עם קבלנים מקומיים, מתקין משאבה סולארית טבולה, בונה מגדל בגובה 10 מטר ומפזר את המים בכפר עד 15 ברזים.
claims.quote: Collaborating with local contractors, we drill into the aquifer, install a submersible solar pump, build a 10-meter tower, and distribute the water throughout the village to up to 15 taps.

claims.quote: Innovation: Africa is a non-profit, non-governmental organization that was established in 2008, by its Founder & CEO, Sivan Yaari.

claims.quote: Over 400 million people across Africa do not have access to clean water. They remain trapped in poverty and disease, without education or economic opportunities.

claims.text: לפי JNS, בעיקר נשים וילדים מופקדים על השגת מים ולעיתים הולכים מרחקים עצומים למקורות מים פתוחים שמזוהמים, מה שמותיר להם מעט זמן ללימודים.

claims.quote: Our job was to make sure that everything was working. We found that most of the generators were not working for two reasons.
